paragraphs.heading: What an earthquake is
paragraphs.text: An earthquake is the shaking of Earth's surface that follows a sudden release of energy, a release that sends out seismic waves. Some earthquakes are too weak to be felt. Others are violent enough to throw objects and people into the air and to bring destruction to whole cities. In its broadest sense, the word covers any seismic event that produces seismic waves, whether it is natural or caused by humans.

paragraphs.heading: Where they come from
paragraphs.text: Most earthquakes are caused by the rupture of geological faults. Others come from volcanic activity, landslides, mine blasts, fracking and nuclear tests. The point where the rupture first starts is called the hypocenter, or focus. Straight above that point, at ground level, lies the epicenter.

paragraphs.heading: Stick, then slip
paragraphs.text: A tectonic earthquake can happen anywhere there is enough stored elastic strain energy to drive a fracture along a fault plane. The two sides of a fault slide past each other smoothly only when the fault surface has no irregularities, called asperities, to raise the frictional resistance. Most fault surfaces do have them, and the result is a kind of stick-slip behavior. Once the fault has locked, the plates keep moving relative to each other, and stress and stored strain energy grow in the rock around the fault surface. That goes on until the stress is high enough to break through the asperity. The locked part of the fault then slides suddenly and the stored energy is let go.

paragraphs.heading: The elastic-rebound theory
paragraphs.text: This pattern has a name. A slow build-up of strain and stress, broken now and then by sudden earthquake failure, is what the elastic-rebound theory describes. The released energy takes three forms: radiated seismic waves, heat from friction on the fault surface, and cracks opened in the rock.

paragraphs.heading: Where the energy goes
paragraphs.text: It is estimated that no more than 10 percent of the total energy of an earthquake is radiated as seismic energy. Most of the energy goes into making the fracture grow or is turned into heat by friction. Earthquakes therefore reduce the elastic potential energy Earth has available, and they raise its temperature. These changes are negligible next to the flow of heat out of Earth's deep interior by conduction and convection.

paragraphs.heading: The largest and the deadliest
paragraphs.text: The largest earthquake ever measured on a seismograph was the 1960 Chilean earthquake, which reached magnitude 9.5 on 22 May 1960. It released roughly twice the energy of the next most powerful one, the Good Friday earthquake of 1964 in Alaska. The ten largest recorded earthquakes were all megathrust earthquakes, yet only one of them, the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake, is also among the deadliest in history. The earthquakes that took the most lives were powerful, but they were deadly because they struck close to heavily populated areas or to the ocean, where earthquakes often create tsunamis.

paragraphs.heading: What follows the shaking
paragraphs.text: Earthquakes can bring ground shaking and soil liquefaction, and they can trigger landslides. When a large earthquake has its epicenter offshore, the seabed may be moved enough to cause a tsunami. People manage the risk through prediction, forecasting and preparedness, which includes seismic retrofitting and the earthquake engineering that designs structures able to withstand shaking.
